nameStory: The name "albida" comes from Latin meaning "whitish," referring to the pale, bleached appearance this green alga can take on when it dries out or grows in very bright conditions. While most green algae stay vibrant green, this species has earned its name by sometimes looking almost ghostly white along rocky shores.
description: Whitish green hair alga is a marine green alga that forms delicate, hair-like tufts clinging to rocks in the intertidal zone. It grows in small, wispy clusters that can reach 2-4 inches tall, looking like tiny green (or whitish-green) pom-poms attached to hard surfaces. This is a simple plant without true roots, stems, or leaves - just branching filaments that do all the work of photosynthesis. When submerged, it sways gracefully in the current like underwater grass.

idTips.label: Branching pattern
idTips.description: Forms repeatedly branching, hair-thin filaments that feel slippery and somewhat coarse between your fingers, unlike the silky smoothness of some other marine algae

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Ranges from bright green when wet and healthy to pale whitish-green or even bleached white when dried or stressed, giving it a faded appearance

idTips.label: Texture when wet
idTips.description: Feels slippery and slightly rough, not as slimy as sea lettuce but not as crisp as rockweed - somewhere in between

idTips.label: Growth form
idTips.description: Grows in small tufts or cushions firmly attached to rock surfaces, each tuft typically 1-4 inches tall and roughly circular in outline

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Always found attached to hard surfaces like rocks, never free-floating, and typically in areas that get regular wave action

habitat: Look for this alga attached to rocks and hard surfaces in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky coasts, particularly in areas with good wave action and water circulation. It prefers the middle to lower intertidal zones where it gets regularly submerged but also experiences some exposure to air during low tides. You'll often find it growing alongside barnacles, mussels, and other marine life on exposed granite and metamorphic rock faces.

seasonality.spring: Growth begins to pick up as water temperatures rise and daylight increases. Fresh, bright green growth is most noticeable during spring tides when you can access lower intertidal areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most vibrant coloration and fullest development. This is the best time to observe the characteristic branching pattern and feel the texture.
seasonality.fall: Still actively growing but may start showing more of the whitish coloration that gives it its name. Storm activity can make observation challenging but also exposes normally submerged populations.
seasonality.winter: Growth slows significantly in cold water, and existing growth may appear more bleached or whitish. Winter storms can reduce populations, but established clumps persist on protected rock faces.

funFact: This tiny alga is essentially immortal - individual filaments can keep growing indefinitely by adding new cells at their tips, and some researchers believe certain clumps could theoretically be hundreds of years old, quietly growing on the same rock through countless storms and tides.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other hair-like marine algae, but the key difference is the whitish cast this species develops - if you see green filamentous alga that looks somewhat faded or bleached, especially in bright sunny spots, you're likely looking at whitish green hair alga rather than its more consistently green relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Note that this species is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, so you're much more likely to encounter its close relatives like green pin-cushion alga. Many beachgoers dismiss all "green stringy stuff" as seaweed, but these filamentous algae are actually quite diverse and play important roles in marine ecosystems as food and shelter for small creatures.
compareHints: Compared to green pin-cushion alga, this species tends to be less densely branched and shows the characteristic whitish coloration that its relatives typically don't develop. Graceful green hair alga is usually more delicately branched and maintains consistent green coloration, while whitish green hair alga has a coarser texture and that telltale faded appearance. The branching in this species also tends to be somewhat more irregular than the neat, cushion-like growth of its pin-cushion relative.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Green pin-cushion algae forms much more compact, defined cushions compared to its cousin graceful green hair algae, which grows in loose, flowing strands.
Graceful green hair differs from its Cladophora relatives by its exceptionally fine, silky texture and preference for the cleanest water conditions.
